questions.q: Which of these sets is NOT closed under subtraction?
o: the set N of natural numbers
the set Q of rational numbers
the set R of real numbers
questions.x: 2 − 5 = −3 is not a natural number, so N is not closed under subtraction. The difference of two integers, two rationals or two reals stays in the same set.

questions.q: Which of these statements is a contradiction, that is, false for every choice of truth values of p and q?
questions.x: p ∧ ~q is true exactly when p → q is false, so (p → q) ∧ (p ∧ ~q) is always false. Joining the same two parts with ∨ gives a tautology; ~p ∧ (p ∨ q) is true when p is false and q true, and p ∧ (q → p) is true when p is true.

questions.q: What is the inverse of f(x) = ∛(x − 2) + 1?
What is the range of f(x) = 3 − x², x ∈ ℝ?
questions.x: x² ≥ 0, so 3 − x² ≤ 3, and the value 3 is reached at x = 0; every smaller value is reached as well. The range is (−∞, 3].

questions.q: lim(x→0) sin(x²)/x equals:
questions.x: sin(x²)/x = x · sin(x²)/x². As x → 0, sin(x²)/x² → 1 and x → 0, so the limit is 0 × 1 = 0. Treating it like (sin x)/x gives the trap answer 1.

questions.q: A is a skew-symmetric matrix of order 3. What is |A|?
questions.x: Aᵗ = −A, so |A| = |Aᵗ| = |−A| = (−1)³|A| = −|A|, hence |A| = 0. The argument needs odd order: the 2 × 2 skew-symmetric matrix [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] has determinant 1.

questions.q: Two real numbers have sum 12. What is the least possible value of the sum of their squares?
questions.x: With numbers x and 12 − x, S = x² + (12 − x)² = 2x² − 24x + 144 = 2(x − 6)² + 72, least 72 at x = 6. Check: 6² + 6² = 72, while 5² + 7² = 74. 36 is the square of one number only.

questions.q: What is the solution set of x^(2/3) − 5x^(1/3) + 4 = 0?
questions.x: Put y = x^(1/3): y² − 5y + 4 = 0 gives y = 1 or y = 4, so x = 1³ = 1 or x = 4³ = 64. Check: 64^(2/3) − 5 × 64^(1/3) + 4 = 16 − 20 + 4 = 0. Stopping at the values of y gives {1, 4}.

questions.q: Distinct positive numbers a, b, c are in H.P. Then a/(b + c), b/(c + a), c/(a + b) are in
questions.x: Reciprocals: (b + c)/a = (a + b + c)/a − 1, and similarly for the others. Since 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P., so are (a + b + c)/a − 1, (a + b + c)/b − 1, (a + b + c)/c − 1, so the given numbers are in H.P. Check with 1, 1/2, 1/3: the reciprocals are 5/6, 8/3, 9/2, with common difference 11/6.

questions.q: A loan of Rs. 3250 is repaid in monthly instalments: Rs. 20 in the first month, and each month Rs. 15 more than the month before. How many months does it take?
How many positive divisors of 360 are even?
questions.x: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. An even divisor has 2ᵃ with a = 1, 2 or 3 (3 choices), 3ᵇ with b = 0, 1, 2 (3 choices) and 5ᶜ with c = 0, 1 (2 choices): 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. Check: 360 has 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 divisors, of which 3 × 2 = 6 are odd, and 24 − 6 = 18.

questions.q: Which term in the expansion of (x² + 1/x)⁹ is independent of x?
questions.x: The general term is ⁹Cᵣ (x²)^(9 − r) (1/x)ʳ = ⁹Cᵣ x^(18 − 3r). Independence needs 18 − 3r = 0, so r = 6, and T(r + 1) is the 7th term (it equals ⁹C₆ = 84). Answering the 6th term confuses r with the term number.

questions.q: The angles are in radians. Which of these has the greatest value?
questions.x: 1 rad ≈ 57°, 2 rad ≈ 115°, 3 rad ≈ 172° and 4 rad ≈ 229°. sin 2 = sin(180° − 115°) = sin 65° is larger than sin 57°; sin 3 = sin 8° is small and sin 4 is negative. Reading the angles as degrees would wrongly pick sin 4.

questions.q: For every θ, sin θ cos θ cos 2θ equals:
questions.x: sin θ cos θ = (1/2) sin 2θ, and (1/2) sin 2θ cos 2θ = (1/4) sin 4θ. Each use of the double-angle formula brings a factor 1/2; using it only once gives (1/2) sin 4θ.

questions.q: What is the value of cos 105° + cos 15°?
questions.x: cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2) = 2 cos 60° cos 45° = 2 × 1/2 × √2/2 = √2/2. Using sin 60° in place of cos 60° gives √6/2.

questions.q: At which points does the graph of y = tan x cross the x-axis? (k ∈ ℤ)
questions.x: tan x = 0 when sin x = 0, that is at x = kπ. The lines x = (2k + 1)π/2 are the vertical asymptotes, where cos x = 0. x = 2kπ misses the zeros at odd multiples of π.

questions.q: Two vertical poles of heights 15 m and 25 m stand on level ground 10√3 m apart. What is the angle of elevation of the top of the taller pole from the top of the shorter one?
questions.x: The rise is 25 − 15 = 10 m over a horizontal distance of 10√3 m, so tan θ = 1/√3 and θ = 30°. Using tan θ = √3 (run over rise) gives 60°.

questions.q: On the interval 0 < x < 1, the graph of y = sin⁻¹x is:
questions.x: y′ = 1/√(1 − x²) > 0, so the graph rises; y″ = x/(1 − x²)^(3/2) > 0 for 0 < x < 1, so it bends upward and becomes vertical at (1, π/2). Mixing it up with y = sin x (concave down there) gives the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: Which statement about f(x) = x|x| at x = 0 is true?
o: f is continuous but not differentiable at 0
f is differentiable at 0 and f′(0) = 1
f is differentiable at 0 and f′(0) = 0
questions.x: [f(0 + h) − f(0)]/h = h|h|/h = |h|, which tends to 0 from both sides, so f′(0) = 0. Unlike |x|, the extra factor x removes the corner: the curve is x² for x ≥ 0 and −x² for x < 0.

questions.q: The point (1, 1) lies on the curve x²y + y³ = 2. What is dy/dx at this point?
questions.x: Differentiate: 2xy + x² y′ + 3y² y′ = 0. At (1, 1): 2 + y′ + 3y′ = 0, so y′ = −1/2. Dropping the x² y′ part of the product rule gives 2 + 3y′ = 0, i.e. −2/3.

questions.q: What is the value of lim(h→0) cos(π/2 + h)/h?
questions.x: Since cos(π/2) = 0, the limit is [cos(π/2 + h) − cos(π/2)]/h, the derivative of cos x at π/2, which is −sin(π/2) = −1. Directly: cos(π/2 + h) = −sin h and (−sin h)/h → −1.

questions.q: ∫ x/(1 + x⁴) dx equals:
questions.x: Put u = x², du = 2x dx: ½∫du/(1 + u²) = ½ tan⁻¹u + C = ½ tan⁻¹(x²) + C. ¼ ln(1 + x⁴) would need x³ in the numerator.

questions.q: To find ∫ x cos 3x dx by parts with u = x and dv = cos 3x dx, the function v is:
questions.x: v = ∫cos 3x dx = (1/3) sin 3x, because d/dx sin 3x = 3 cos 3x. Differentiating instead of integrating gives −3 sin 3x, and forgetting the 1/3 gives sin 3x.

questions.q: A particle slows down so that dv/dt = −v², with v in m/s and t in s. If v = 1 m/s at t = 0, how far does it travel from t = 0 to t = 3 s?
questions.x: Separate: −dv/v² = dt gives 1/v = t + 1, so v = 1/(t + 1) > 0. Distance = ∫₀³ dt/(t + 1) = ln 4 = 2 ln 2 m. Stopping at t = 1 gives ln 2.

questions.q: The lines y = mx + 1 and y = 2x − 3 meet on the x-axis. What is m?
questions.x: y = 2x − 3 meets the x-axis at (3/2, 0). Then 0 = (3/2)m + 1 gives m = −2/3.

questions.q: The region y ≥ 1, x + y ≤ 5, x − y ≥ −1 is a triangle. What is its area?
questions.x: Corners: y = 1 with x − y = −1 gives (0, 1); y = 1 with x + y = 5 gives (4, 1); x + y = 5 with x − y = −1 gives (2, 3). Base 4 and height 2, so the area is ½ × 4 × 2 = 4.

questions.q: A point moves so that its distance from (0, 2) equals its distance from the x-axis. What is the equation of its path?
questions.x: √(x² + (y − 2)²) = |y| gives x² − 4y + 4 = 0, i.e. x² = 4(y − 1). Its vertex (0, 1) lies halfway between the focus (0, 2) and the directrix y = 0.

questions.q: What is the length of the intercept that the circle x² + y² − 4x − 6y − 7 = 0 cuts off on the y-axis?
questions.x: Put x = 0: y² − 6y − 7 = 0, so y = 7 or y = −1 and the intercept is 7 − (−1) = 8. Check: 2√(f² − c) = 2√(9 + 7) = 8.

questions.q: What is the angle between a diagonal of a cube and an edge of the cube drawn from the same corner?
questions.x: Take the unit cube at the origin: diagonal i + j + k, edge i. cos θ = 1/(√3 × 1) = 1/√3. cos⁻¹(√2/√3) is the angle between the diagonal and a face diagonal, and cos⁻¹(1/3) the angle between two diagonals.

questions.q: Use the trapezium rule with h = π/2 to estimate ∫₀^π sin x dx.
questions.x: The ordinates at 0, π/2 and π are 0, 1 and 0, so the estimate is (h/2)[0 + 0 + 2(1)] = (π/4)(2) = π/2. The exact value is 2, so this estimate is too small.

questions.q: p is the momentum and K the kinetic energy of a body. The quantity p²/K has the dimensions of:
questions.x: p² = [M²L²T⁻²] and K = [ML²T⁻²], so p²/K = [M], a mass; indeed K = p²/2m gives p²/K = 2m. Inverting the ratio gives [M⁻¹].

questions.q: Point P has coordinates (1, 2) m and point Q has coordinates (4, 6) m. The magnitude of the displacement from P to Q is:
questions.x: PQ = (4 − 1)î + (6 − 2)ĵ = 3î + 4ĵ, so |PQ| = √(9 + 16) = 5 m. Adding the position vectors gives (5, 8) and √89 m; the size of Q's position vector alone is √52 m.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg ball dropped from a height of 5 m rebounds to a height of 1.25 m. It is in contact with the floor for 0.1 s. Ignoring air resistance and the ball's weight during the contact, and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the average force of the floor on the ball is:
questions.x: Speed before impact = √(2 × 10 × 5) = 10 m s⁻¹ downward; after = √(2 × 10 × 1.25) = 5 m s⁻¹ upward. Δp = 0.5 × (10 + 5) = 7.5 N s, so F = 7.5/0.1 = 75 N. Subtracting the speeds, as if both were in the same direction, gives 25 N.

questions.q: Ball X moving at 5 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with ball Y at rest. After the collision X continues forward at 1 m s⁻¹. The velocity of Y just after the collision is:
questions.x: In an elastic head-on collision the speed of separation equals the speed of approach: v_Y − 1 = 5 − 0, so v_Y = 6 m s⁻¹. (Momentum then fixes m_X/m_Y = 1.5, consistent with the elastic formula.) Treating the masses as equal and using 5 − 1 gives 4 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A body falls freely in a vacuum near the Earth's surface. Which quantity stays constant during its fall?
questions.x: In free fall the only force is the weight, so the acceleration is constant at g. Velocity, momentum and kinetic energy all increase as it falls.

questions.q: A constant net force accelerates a body from rest along a straight line. The power delivered by the force:
o: Increases in proportion to the time
Increases in proportion to the square of the time
questions.x: P = Fv, and with a constant force v = at grows in proportion to t, so P = Fat ∝ t. Thinking constant force means constant power is the usual error; it is the kinetic energy that grows as t².

questions.q: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of:
questions.x: Angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt, the rate of change of angular velocity. The rate of change of angular displacement is the angular velocity itself.

questions.q: Honey flows much more easily when it is warmed. This shows that, as the temperature of a liquid rises, its viscosity:
questions.x: Warm honey pours faster, so its resistance to flow, the viscosity, has fallen: the viscosity of a liquid decreases as its temperature rises. (For gases the change is the other way, which is the usual source of confusion.)

questions.q: A mass on a spring oscillates with amplitude x₀. It is replaced by a mass four times as large on the same spring, oscillating with the same amplitude x₀. Compared with before:
o: The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is halved
The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is unchanged
The total energy is four times as large and the maximum speed is unchanged
The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is doubled
questions.x: Total energy = ½kx₀² depends only on k and x₀, so it is unchanged. Then ½mv_max² is the same, so v_max ∝ 1/√m and quadrupling m halves it (check: ω = √(k/m) halves, v_max = ωx₀).

questions.q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 3 beats per second with a 400 Hz fork and 5 beats per second with a 408 Hz fork. Its frequency is:
questions.x: From the first fork the frequency is 397 or 403 Hz; from the second, 403 or 413 Hz. Only 403 Hz fits both (check: 403 − 400 = 3 and 408 − 403 = 5). 397 Hz would give 11 beats with the 408 Hz fork.

questions.q: In the time a particle of the medium completes one full vibration, a progressive wave travels a distance of:
questions.x: One vibration takes one period T, and in time T the wave moves vT = λ, one wavelength. Four times the amplitude is the distance the particle itself moves in one vibration, not the wave.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm travels in air. Two points lie on the same ray, 150 nm apart. What is the phase difference between the vibrations at the two points?
questions.x: Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference = 2π × 150/600 = π/2 rad, since 150 nm is a quarter of a wavelength. Taking a quarter wavelength as half a cycle gives π rad.

questions.q: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The eyepiece is changed so that the magnifying power in normal adjustment becomes 40. What is the new distance between the lenses?
questions.x: M = fₒ/fₑ, so the new eyepiece has fₑ = 100/40 = 2.5 cm. In normal adjustment the length is fₒ + fₑ = 102.5 cm. Doubling the eyepiece focal length instead gives 110 cm.

questions.q: The internal energy of a fixed mass of an ideal gas depends only on its:
questions.x: In an ideal gas there are no forces between molecules, so the internal energy is just the kinetic energy of the molecules, which depends only on temperature.

questions.q: A Carnot engine could have an efficiency of 100% only if:
o: Its source and sink were at the same temperature
Its sink were at absolute zero, which cannot be reached
questions.x: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ equals 1 only when T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached, so even an ideal engine cannot reach 100%. Equal temperatures give zero efficiency.

questions.q: An alpha particle (charge +2e) starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. The kinetic energy it gains is:
questions.x: KE = qV = 2e × 1000 V = 2000 eV (= 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ J). Treating it as having charge e gives 1000 eV.

questions.q: A charge of +4 nC is at point P and a charge of −2 nC is at point Q, 30 cm away. At what point on the segment PQ is the electric potential zero?
questions.x: V = 0 where k(4)/x = k(2)/(30 − x): 4(30 − x) = 2x, so x = 20 cm from P. Check: 4/20 = 2/10 = 0.2. Placing the point nearer the larger charge gives 10 cm.

questions.q: A battery of internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to an external load of 4 Ω. The fraction of the power produced by the battery that is delivered to the load is:
questions.x: The same current flows through r and R, so the fraction is I²R / I²(R + r) = 4/5 = 80%. The 20% is the share wasted inside the battery.

questions.q: One kilowatt-hour (the 'unit' on an electricity bill) is equal to:
A long solenoid is stretched to twice its length. The number of turns, the radius and the current stay the same. The magnetic field inside it becomes:
o: One quarter of its original value
questions.x: B = μ₀nI with n = N/L. Doubling L with N fixed halves n, so B halves. Thinking only the total number of turns matters gives unchanged.

questions.q: An ideal ammeter should have:
o: Infinite resistance, and be connected in parallel
Zero resistance, and be connected in parallel
Zero resistance, and be connected in series
Infinite resistance, and be connected in series
questions.x: An ammeter goes in series so the current to be measured passes through it, and it should have no resistance so it does not reduce that current. The ideal voltmeter is the opposite: infinite resistance, in parallel.

questions.q: An inductor of 0.25 H stores 2 J of energy in its magnetic field. The current through it is:
questions.x: U = ½LI², so I² = 2U/L = 4/0.25 = 16 and I = 4 A. Forgetting the square root gives 16 A; dropping the ½ gives I² = 8, about 2.8 A.

questions.q: The reactance of a capacitor to a steady direct current (frequency zero) is:
o: Equal to its reactance at 50 Hz
Infinitely large, so the capacitor blocks steady DC once charged
questions.x: XC = 1/(2πfC), and as f → 0, XC → ∞. A steady current cannot pass through the insulating gap once the capacitor is charged. A zero reactance at DC belongs to an inductor.

questions.q: A wire obeys Hooke's law. The load on it is doubled, still within the proportional limit. The elastic potential energy stored in the wire becomes:
questions.x: Energy stored = ½ × F × extension, and the extension is proportional to F, so the energy is proportional to F². Doubling F doubles the extension too, so the energy becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times. Forgetting that the extension also doubles gives 2 times.

questions.q: In an NPN transistor, the middle region, which is very thin and lightly doped, is the:
questions.x: The base is the thin, lightly doped middle layer, so most charge carriers from the emitter pass through it to the collector and the base current is small. The emitter is heavily doped and the collector is the largest region.

questions.q: According to the relation m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²), as the speed of a body with rest mass m₀ approaches the speed of light, its mass:
o: Increases without limit, so the body can never reach the speed of light
questions.x: As v → c the denominator √(1 − v²/c²) → 0, so m grows without limit and an unlimited force or energy would be needed for further acceleration; no body with rest mass can reach c. At low speeds m ≈ m₀.

questions.q: A high-energy gamma-ray photon can change into an electron-positron pair only when it passes close to a heavy nucleus, not in empty space. The nucleus is needed mainly to:
o: Supply the charge of the electron
Take up some momentum so that momentum is conserved
Supply the rest-mass energy of the pair
Slow the photon down below the speed of light
questions.x: In empty space a photon cannot turn into a pair while conserving both energy and momentum; a nearby nucleus recoils and takes the extra momentum, while taking very little energy. The pair's charges cancel (−e and +e), and the energy comes from the photon itself.

questions.q: X-rays pass undeflected between charged plates and between the poles of a magnet. This shows that X-rays:
questions.x: Electric and magnetic fields deflect only charged particles; X-rays are not deflected, which fits their nature as electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength. Electron beams (cathode rays) are deflected by both fields.

questions.q: The radioactive series that starts with ²³²₉₀Th ends with the stable nucleus ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. The numbers of alpha and beta (β⁻) particles emitted in the whole series are:
questions.x: Only alpha decay changes A: (232 − 208)/4 = 6 alpha particles. These lower Z by 12, to 78, but the final Z is 82, so 82 − 78 = 4 β⁻ decays raised it. Taking the drop in Z (8) as the number of beta decays gives 6 alpha and 8 beta.

questions.q: Before an X-ray image of the stomach and intestines is taken, the patient swallows a 'barium meal'. This is done because barium:
o: Lets X-rays pass through more easily
Absorbs X-rays strongly, so the outline of the soft gut shows clearly
questions.x: Soft tissues absorb X-rays about equally, so the gut barely shows; barium, a heavy element, absorbs X-rays strongly and acts as a contrast medium, so the parts it fills appear clearly on the image. It is not radioactive.

questions.q: How many electrons are present in 1.6 g of methane, CH₄? (H = 1, C = 12; Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 1.6 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1 mol CH₄. Each molecule has 6 + 4 × 1 = 10 electrons, so 1 mol of electrons = 6.02 × 10²³. 6.02 × 10²² is the number of molecules (forgot the 10 electrons per molecule), and 3.01 × 10²³ is the number of atoms.

questions.q: A mixture gives two spots on a paper chromatogram, 2.0 cm and 5.0 cm from the base line, when the solvent front has moved 8.0 cm. In the same solvent, pure substances have Rf values P 0.25, Q 0.40, R 0.625 and S 0.75. The mixture contains:
questions.x: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front: 2.0/8.0 = 0.25 (P) and 5.0/8.0 = 0.625 (R). Measuring the spots from the solvent front instead of the base line gives 0.75 and 0.375, pointing wrongly to S and Q.

questions.q: At what temperature will oxygen molecules have the same root-mean-square speed as hydrogen molecules at 27 °C? (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.x: c(rms) = √(3RT/M), so equal speeds need equal T/M: T/32 = 300/2, so T = 4800 K. Using the square-root ratio (×4) gives 1200 K, and dividing instead of multiplying gives 18.75 K.

questions.q: Diamond is extremely hard and has a very high melting point because:
o: Its carbon atoms are held by London forces only
It contains free electrons that bind the atoms
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a continuous three-dimensional network
Its carbon atoms are held by ionic bonds
questions.x: In diamond each sp³ carbon is joined tetrahedrally to four others, so melting or scratching it means breaking many strong covalent bonds. Free delocalised electrons belong to graphite and metals.

questions.q: Bohr's model of the atom could NOT explain:
o: The lines of the hydrogen spectrum
The stability of the hydrogen atom
The spectra of atoms with more than one electron
questions.x: Bohr's model worked well for hydrogen (spectral lines, stability, ionisation energy) but failed for atoms with two or more electrons and for the fine splitting of lines.

questions.q: For oxygen, O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g) has ΔH = −141 kJ mol⁻¹ and O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) has ΔH = +780 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g), and why is the second step endothermic?
o: −921 kJ mol⁻¹; both steps release energy
+921 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron enters a new shell
+639 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron is added to a negative ion and is repelled by it
−639 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron is attracted by the nucleus
questions.x: Adding the steps: −141 + 780 = +639 kJ mol⁻¹. The second electron must be forced onto O⁻, which already carries a negative charge and repels it, so energy is absorbed. +921 comes from adding the magnitudes and ignoring the sign of the first step; O²⁻ has the neon configuration, so no new shell is entered.

questions.q: How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
questions.x: Each carbon is sp² and forms σ bonds to two carbons and one hydrogen: 6 C–C σ plus 6 C–H σ = 12 σ. The six unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to give 3 π bonds (in the Kekulé picture of three C=C). Counting only the C–C σ bonds gives 6 σ.

questions.q: The Born–Haber cycle, used to find the lattice energy of an ionic solid, is an application of:
questions.x: The Born–Haber cycle treats the formation of an ionic solid from its elements as a series of steps whose enthalpy changes must add up to the overall ΔHf; this is Hess's law of constant heat summation.

questions.q: In the Haber process, how is the ammonia separated from the gas mixture leaving the converter?
o: The mixture is passed through water, which dissolves N₂ and H₂
The mixture is cooled so that ammonia liquefies, and the unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled
The ammonia is burnt off and collected as a solid
The N₂ and H₂ are liquefied first and the ammonia gas passes on
questions.x: Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than nitrogen or hydrogen, so cooling liquefies it while N₂ and H₂ stay as gases and are sent back to the converter. Removing NH₃ also keeps pulling the equilibrium to the right. N₂ and H₂ are only slightly soluble in water, and they liquefy at far lower temperatures than NH₃.

questions.q: Which of these species cannot act as a Lewis base?
questions.x: A Lewis base must have a lone pair to donate. NH₃ has one, H₂O has two and Cl⁻ has four, but in CH₄ all four valence pairs of carbon are used in C–H bonds, so it has no lone pair to donate.

questions.q: At 25 °C, a solution has a pH of 9.0. What is its pOH?
questions.x: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.0, so pOH = 14.0 − 9.0 = 5.0. 23 is the slip of adding instead of subtracting.

questions.q: 15 g of KCl is dissolved in 135 g of water. What is the percentage by mass of KCl in the solution?
questions.x: Mass of solution = 15 + 135 = 150 g, so % KCl = 15/150 × 100 = 10%. Dividing by the mass of water (135 g) instead of the mass of solution gives the tempting 11.1%.

questions.q: E° values: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Ni²⁺/Ni −0.25 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V. Which metal can liberate hydrogen from 1 mol dm⁻³ HCl but cannot displace iron from a solution of Fe²⁺ ions?
questions.x: To liberate H₂ the metal's E° must be below 0.00 V; to fail to displace iron it must be above −0.44 V. Only nickel (−0.25 V) fits. Zinc and magnesium do both; copper does neither.

questions.q: At 300 K, 2.303RT = 5.74 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction by 11.48 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K without changing A. By what factor does the rate constant increase?
questions.x: From k = A e^(−Ea/RT), log(k₂/k₁) = ΔEa/(2.303RT) = 11.48/5.74 = 2, so k₂/k₁ = 10² = 100. Stopping at 2 forgets to take the antilog.

questions.q: Which oxide reacts with water to give a strongly alkaline solution (pH about 13 to 14)?
questions.x: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, a soluble strong base. MgO is only slightly soluble and gives a weakly alkaline solution (pH about 9–10); Al₂O₃ is insoluble, and P₄O₁₀ gives the acid H₃PO₄.

questions.q: Which Group 2 oxide is the most basic?
questions.x: Basic character of Group 2 oxides increases down the group as the metal becomes more electropositive, so BaO is the most basic of these (it gives the strong base Ba(OH)₂). MgO is only weakly basic.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of boron in borax, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O?
questions.x: Water of crystallisation is neutral, so in Na₂B₄O₇: 2(+1) + 4x + 7(−2) = 0, giving 4x = 12 and x = +3. Forgetting the factor of 4 on boron or miscounting the oxygens gives +4 or +5.

questions.q: Phosphorus pentachloride is treated with a limited amount of water. The products are:
questions.x: Partial hydrolysis replaces two Cl atoms by one O: PCl₅ + H₂O → POCl₃ + 2HCl. H₃PO₄ forms only with excess water, so it is the tempting answer if the word limited is ignored; H₃PO₃ comes from PCl₃, not PCl₅.

questions.q: In making potassium permanganate, MnO₂ is fused with KOH in air to give a green compound X; X is then oxidised to the purple compound Y. X and Y, with the oxidation states of Mn, are:
questions.x: 2MnO₂ + 4KOH + O₂ → 2K₂MnO₄ + 2H₂O gives green potassium manganate (Mn +6); oxidising it removes one more electron to give purple KMnO₄ (Mn +7). Swapping the two compounds forgets that the green manganate comes first.

questions.q: EDTA⁴⁻ binds a metal ion through two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms. It is therefore a:
questions.x: Six donor atoms (2 N + 4 O) bind one metal ion, so EDTA is hexadentate and forms very stable chelates. Counting only the four carboxylate oxygens gives tetradentate.

questions.q: In the methyl carbanion, CH₃⁻, the carbon atom is:
o: sp² hybridised, with a trigonal planar shape
sp hybridised, with a linear shape
sp³ hybridised, with a square planar shape
sp³ hybridised, with a pyramidal shape
questions.x: The carbanion carbon has three bond pairs and one lone pair, four electron domains, so it is sp³ and pyramidal like NH₃. sp² and planar describes the carbocation CH₃⁺, which has no lone pair; that is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: 2-Bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃, is heated with sodium metal in dry ether (Wurtz reaction). The alkane formed is:
questions.x: The two carbons that carried bromine join: (CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂, named 2,3-dimethylbutane. Hexane would come from 1-bromopropane, where the chain ends join.

questions.q: The carbon–carbon bond order in benzene is:
questions.x: Six π electrons (three π bonds' worth) are shared equally over six C–C bonds, so each bond is a σ bond plus half a π bond: order 1.5. Orders 1 or 2 describe the separate bonds of a single Kekulé structure.

questions.q: Bromoethane is heated with potassium cyanide in ethanol. The main organic product is:
questions.x: CN⁻ is a nucleophile and replaces Br⁻: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻, adding one carbon to the chain. CH₃CN forgets that the cyanide carbon is added rather than swapped for a carbon of the ethyl group.

questions.q: Phenol is treated with concentrated nitric acid (in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid). The main product is:
questions.x: The –OH group strongly activates the ring, so with concentrated acid all three ortho and para positions are nitrated. Dilute nitric acid gives only the mononitrophenols; –OH is not a meta director.

questions.q: A primary alcohol is oxidised gently with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, and the product is distilled off as it forms. The product belongs to the class of:
questions.x: RCH₂OH loses two hydrogens to give RCHO, an aldehyde; removing it at once stops further oxidation to the acid. Ketones come from secondary alcohols.

questions.q: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid (60 g mol⁻¹) is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄, and 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate (88 g mol⁻¹) is obtained. The percentage yield is:
questions.x: 0.10 mol of acid can give at most 0.10 mol = 8.8 g of ester; 5.28/8.8 × 100 = 60%. Dividing the ester mass by the acid mass (5.28/6.0) gives 88%, and 40% is the part not obtained.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propanal into propan-1-ol?
questions.x: Converting an aldehyde to a primary alcohol is a reduction, and NaBH₄ supplies hydride ions. Dichromate and Tollens' reagent are oxidising agents that would give propanoic acid, the opposite change.

questions.q: What is the index of hydrogen deficiency (IHD) of C₆H₁₁Cl?
questions.x: A halogen counts like a hydrogen: IHD = (2C + 2 − H − X)/2 = (12 + 2 − 11 − 1)/2 = 1, so the molecule has one ring or one double bond (for example chlorocyclohexane). Leaving the Cl out and reading the formula as C₆H₁₀ gives 2, the most tempting slip.

questions.q: A 500 cm³ water sample contains 0.050 mg of lead. The safe limit for lead in drinking water is taken as 0.010 mg dm⁻³. The lead concentration of the sample is how many times this limit?
questions.x: 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³, so the concentration is 0.050/0.500 = 0.10 mg dm⁻³, which is 0.10/0.010 = 10 times the limit. Forgetting to convert the volume (0.050/0.010) gives 5.

questions.q: When RAM is full, the operating system uses part of the hard disk as if it were extra RAM. This is called:
questions.x: Virtual memory lets the operating system move parts of programs between RAM and a space on the disk, so more can run than RAM alone allows. Cache memory is a small fast memory between the CPU and RAM, not space on the disk.

questions.q: A teacher wants the whole class to see her computer screen enlarged on a white wall. Which output device should she use?
questions.x: A multimedia projector takes the computer's display output and throws a large image on a wall or screen. A scanner and a web camera are input devices, and a printer gives paper output.

questions.q: A client-server network has only one server, which holds all the shared files. What happens if this server fails?
o: The clients cannot reach the shared files and services
The clients start sharing files peer-to-peer automatically
Nothing, because each client keeps a copy of the server's files
questions.x: In a client-server network, the shared files and services live on the server, so its failure cuts the clients off from them. Clients do not automatically turn into a peer-to-peer network.

questions.q: Counting from layer 1 upward, which list gives the first four OSI layers in the correct order?
questions.x: Layer 1 is Physical, layer 2 Data Link, layer 3 Network and layer 4 Transport, followed by Session, Presentation and Application. Swapping Network and Transport puts end-to-end delivery below routing, which is wrong.

questions.q: In networking, the word "node" means:
o: Only the main server of the network
The cable that joins two computers
Any device connected to the network, such as a computer or printer
questions.x: A node is any device attached to a network that can send, receive or pass on data: a computer, printer, switch and so on. A server is one kind of node, not the only one.

questions.q: A bank hires a security expert who, with the bank's written permission, tries to break into its network to find weak points before criminals do. This is:
questions.x: Ethical hacking (penetration testing) is done with the owner's permission to find and fix weaknesses. The same actions without permission would be unauthorised access, a crime.

questions.q: In a shared online document, a reviewer wants to give feedback on a sentence without changing the text itself. What should she add?
questions.x: A comment attaches a note to the selected text for collaborators to read and reply to, leaving the text unchanged. A footnote becomes part of the document's printed content.

questions.q: Many home security cameras connected to the Internet are left with their factory-set default passwords. What is the main risk?
o: The cameras will use too little electricity
The cameras will be unable to connect to Wi-Fi
Attackers may log in to watch or control the cameras
The pictures from the cameras will become blurred
questions.x: Default passwords are widely known, so attackers can take over such IoT devices; changing the password is a basic IoT safety step. Passwords do not affect power use or picture quality.

questions.q: In a Windows file search, the wildcard `?` stands for exactly one character. Which file matches the pattern `r?t.txt`?
questions.x: `r?t.txt` needs r, then one character, then t, with the extension .txt, so `rat.txt` matches. `rt.txt` has no character in between, `rant.txt` has two, and `rat.doc` has the wrong extension.

questions.q: A footer must show the correct page number on every page, even after more pages are added. What should be inserted in the footer?
questions.x: A page-number field is filled in automatically with each page's own number and updates when pages change. A number typed by hand in the footer would show the same number on every page.

questions.q: Order(OrderNo, Date, CustID, CustName, ProductID, ProductName, Qty) has the key (OrderNo, ProductID), with OrderNo → Date, OrderNo → CustID, CustID → CustName, ProductID → ProductName and (OrderNo, ProductID) → Qty. How many tables result when it is normalised to 3NF in the usual way?
questions.x: The tables are OrderHead(OrderNo, Date, CustID), Customer(CustID, CustName), Product(ProductID, ProductName) and OrderLine(OrderNo, ProductID, Qty): 4. Stopping at 2NF would leave CustName with the order data and give 3.

questions.q: A relation has the functional dependencies P → Q and Q → S. Which dependency must also hold?
questions.x: If each P value fixes one Q value, and each Q value fixes one S value, then each P value fixes one S value, so P → S (transitivity). The reverse directions are not implied.

questions.q: Employee(EmpID, Name, ManagerID) stores in ManagerID the EmpID of each employee's manager, who is also an employee. What does ManagerID refer to?
o: The primary key of a separate Manager table that must be created
The primary key EmpID of the same Employee table
Nothing, since a table cannot refer to itself
A composite key made of EmpID and Name
questions.x: This is a unary (recursive) relationship, so ManagerID is a foreign key that points to EmpID in the same table. No separate Manager table is needed, because managers are employees too.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In Access, the criteria `Like "*o*"` is typed under Title. Which titles are returned?
questions.x: *o* matches any title that contains the letter o anywhere: Optics, Atoms and Geometry. Access's Like ignores letter case, so the capital O of Optics matches too; Mechanics has no o.

questions.q: In the Access query design grid, in which row is a condition such as >500 typed so that only matching records are shown?
questions.x: Conditions go in the Criteria row under the field they test. The Sort row sets the order, the Show box decides whether the field appears, and the Field row names the field.

questions.q: Among the operators `+`, `*`, `=` and `&&`, which has the highest precedence?
questions.x: Multiplication is done before addition, both arithmetic operators come before the logical &&, and assignment = has the lowest precedence of the four.

questions.q: Which format specifier prints a string such as "Lahore"?
questions.x: %s prints the characters of a string until its terminating null character. %c would print only one character.
fputs writes the string exactly as given and adds no space or newline, so the two strings sit side by side: GoodDay. The file is opened once with "w", so the second fputs does not wipe the first.

questions.q: A function is declared as `void show(int n);`. What happens when a program contains the statement `int k = show(4);`?
o: The compiler reports an error, because `show` returns no value
questions.x: A void function returns nothing, so its call cannot be used as a value; the compiler rejects the statement. Passing 4 as an argument does not make 4 the returned value.
c starts at 'p' and moves 2 letters each pass: 'p', 'r', 't'. The next value 'v' is past 't', so the loop stops. pqrst would need c++ instead of c += 2.

questions.q: A marks field should accept whole numbers from 0 to 100. A tester types `abc` into it to check that the program rejects it. What kind of test data is this?
questions.x: Data that the program should refuse, such as letters in a number field, is invalid or erroneous test data. Boundary data would be values at the edges, such as 0, 100 or 101.

questions.q: A programmer adds lines such as `print("x =", x)` at several points in a program to watch how the values change while it runs. What is this?
o: Debugging by printing values at chosen points
questions.x: Printing variables at chosen points lets the programmer see where a value first goes wrong, which is a simple debugging technique. Black-box and acceptance testing look only at inputs and outputs, not at values inside the code.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(10 / 4, 10 // 4.0)
```
questions.x: `/` always gives a float: 2.5. `//` gives the floor, 2, but because one operand (4.0) is a float the result is the float 2.0, not the int 2.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
t = 35
if t > 20:
    msg = "warm"
elif t > 30:
    msg = "hot"
else:
    msg = "cool"
print(msg)
```
questions.x: The conditions are checked from the top and only the first True branch runs: 35 > 20 is True, so msg is "warm" and the `elif` is never checked. hot would need the test `t > 30` to come first.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
x = 5
x = str(x) + "5"
print(int(x) * 2)
```
questions.x: `str(5) + "5"` joins two strings to give "55"; `int("55")` is the number 55, and 55 * 2 = 110. 5555 would be the string "55" repeated, but `int` converted it first.

questions.q: Finding the shortest road route from Lahore to Peshawar, out of all possible routes, is which type of computational problem?
questions.x: The task is to pick the best (shortest) of many possible answers, which makes it an optimisation problem. A decision problem would only ask a yes/no question, such as whether a route under 200 km exists.

questions.q: The domain is all people. S(x) means "x is a student" and L(x) means "x likes chess". Which formula says "Some students like chess"?
questions.x: We need at least one x who is a student and likes chess: ∃x (S(x) ∧ L(x)). ∃x (S(x) → L(x)) is already true if any one person is not a student, so it does not say what is meant.

questions.q: In logic, which symbol stands for disjunction ("or")?
questions.x: ∨ is "or" (disjunction). ∧ is "and" (conjunction), ¬ is "not" and → is "if … then".

questions.q: A library database has 40 articles that contain the word robot, 25 that contain the word sensor, and 10 that contain both. How many articles does the search `robot OR sensor` return?
questions.x: OR returns articles with either word, but the 10 with both must be counted once: 40 + 25 − 10 = 55. 65 counts those 10 twice, and 10 is the answer for `robot AND sensor`.

questions.q: What is the writer's main argument?
o: Athletes should give up hard training and rely on gentle movement
Coaches are mainly to blame for injuries among young athletes
Rest is an essential part of training, because the body improves during recovery
Sleep matters more than training for success in sport
questions.x: The writer says "The improvement comes afterwards, during recovery" and calls rest "the half of training that nobody sees". Hard training is not given up: it is "the signal" that rest answers.

questions.q: According to the passage, how does hard training affect performance the next morning?
o: It makes the athlete stronger at once
It often makes performance worse, as the muscles are tired
It has no effect until a week has passed
It improves speed but weakens strength
questions.x: Hard training "leaves muscles tired and slightly damaged, and performance the next morning is often worse". It does not make a person stronger "on the day it is done".

questions.q: The writer would most likely disapprove of an athlete who:
o: takes a rest day with a short walk and an early night
trains hard on some days and gently on others
eats a proper meal after a hard session
trains hard every day and feels guilty about taking a day off
questions.x: The writer criticises the view that rest days are "something to apologise for" and that training "every day without a break" shows dedication. A walk and an early night fit the advice: "Gentle movement, good sleep and proper meals are part of the work".

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "nagging" most nearly means:
questions.x: "Nagging injuries" come with "heavy legs" and "falling times": they keep troubling the athlete. "Complaining and scolding" is the word's meaning for a person, not for an injury.

questions.q: The tone of the passage as a whole is best described as:
o: firm and corrective, challenging a common belief
light and humorous, poking fun at athletes
uncertain, unable to decide between two views
bitter, blaming coaches for harming athletes
questions.x: The writer states plainly that the usual attitude "misunderstands how the body improves" and that athletes "need to stop treating recovery as time lost". Coaches are mentioned without bitterness, alongside the athletes themselves.

questions.q: Which would be the best title for the passage?
o: How Bricks Are Made in a Village
The Last Farm on the Channel
questions.x: The passage is about the narrator's family at "the very end of a long watercourse" and how lining the channel changed their Thursday nights. There is no quarrel: the father was "never shouting at anyone".

questions.q: According to the narrator, why did so little water reach his family's fields?
o: Their turn was shorter than that of other families
The channel had been lined with bricks too late
Some soaked into the banks and some was taken by neighbours upstream
Their fields lay higher than the rest of the farms
questions.x: Water "had soaked into the earth banks" and "had been quietly taken by neighbours who left their outlets open". Their turn was not shorter: it "lasted as many hours as anyone's".

questions.q: The narrator's boyhood view that the system was fair overlooked the fact that:
o: his family had a longer turn than other farmers
the turns were fixed by his father alone
equal hours of water did not mean equal amounts of water
Thursday nights were the busiest time on the channel
questions.x: As a boy he reasoned "Each family had its turn", but later saw that, though their turn "lasted as many hours as anyone's", the stream was "thin and tired". A longer turn is contradicted by that same sentence.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tired" most nearly means:
questions.x: After passing "thirty farms", the stream was "thin and tired", that is, weak and reduced, in contrast to the "fast and clear" water that comes later. "In need of sleep" is the everyday meaning, used of people.

questions.q: What does the father's going to bed early at the end of the passage most likely show?
o: Relief that he no longer had to guard the water
Anger at the cost of the brick lining
Illness after years of hard work
questions.x: For years he spent Thursday nights "walking the channel with a lantern"; now the water arrives "fast and clear", so he can rest. Disappointment is wrong: the work has solved his problem.
